<explanation>
Based on the project’s file tree and README, here’s how to design a detailed system architecture diagram tailored to garak – an LLM vulnerability scanner and red-teaming tool for generative models.

1. Identify the Project Type and Purpose:
   - This is a command‐line tool that tests large language models (LLMs) by running a variety of probes, detectors, and evaluators to flag vulnerabilities (e.g. hallucination, prompt injection, jailbreaks, toxicity).
   - The README and file structure indicate that garak is built as a modular, plugin-based system. It abstracts components such as probes (attack vectors), detectors (failure detection), generators (LLM interfaces), and harnesses (orchestrators) to run tests and produce detailed reports.

2. Analyze the File Structure:
   - Top-level directories include configuration files (e.g., .github, MANIFEST.in, requirements.txt), documentation (docs/), and core code under the “garak” folder.
   - Inside “garak”, you see modules such as:
     • probes/ – where each probe (e.g., dan, encoding, packagehallucination) is implemented.
     • detectors/ – modules for recognizing specific vulnerability patterns.
     • generators/ – adapters for different LLM APIs (OpenAI, huggingface, replicate, etc.).
     • harnesses/ – modules that coordinate the testing process (e.g., the probewise harness).
     • evaluators/, buffs/, analyze/ – supporting modules for evaluation, pre/post processing, and analysis of results.
   - Supplementary directories like “data” (contains model prompts, configurations, and corpora), “configs”, “resources”, and extensive tests indicate a mature, layered architecture.

3. Extract Insights from the README:
   - The README describes the overall flow: the tool receives CLI parameters (such as model type and name), loads probes (each with recommended detectors), chooses a generator, and passes them to a harness that runs tests. After generations, evaluators and loggers analyze the outcomes and produce reports.
   - It also explains how plugins are designed by inheriting from base classes (with each major category – probes, detectors, generators, etc. – having its own base file), reinforcing the modular, extensible nature of the system.

4. Outline the Main Components for the System Design Diagram:
   a. Entry Point & CLI:
      - Command-line script (garak/__main__.py and garak/cli.py) that parses user options and initializes the scan.
   b. Plugin Management & Core Modules:
      - Probes: Located in garak/probes/, these modules generate test scenarios/attack prompts.
      - Detectors: Located in garak/detectors/, these modules assess responses for vulnerabilities.
      - Generators: Located in garak/generators/, this component interfaces with external LLMs (using providers like OpenAI, Hugging Face, Replicate, etc.).
      - Harnesses: Found in garak/harnesses/, these orchestrate the testing by integrating inputs from probes and generators.
      - Evaluators: Found in garak/evaluators/, these modules compile and report the results from probes/detectors.
   c. Data & Configuration:
      - Configurations: The “configs” folder holds various YAML configurations detailing how tests should run.
      - Data Resources: The “data” directory contains ancillary data (e.g., prompt templates, payloads) used by the probes and detectors.
   d. Logging & Reporting:
      - Logging components (e.g., garak.log, analysis scripts under garak/analyze/) capture runtime diagnostics.
      - Report generation (JSONL output, hit logs) to evaluate probe outcomes.

5. Relationships and Interactions:
   - The CLI feeds user parameters into a “Controller” (entry point) that selects appropriate plugins from probes, detectors, generators, and harnesses.
   - The selected generator communicates with LLM endpoints (via REST/API, local inference with ggml, etc.) to process each probe.
   - The harness coordinates the flow: it submits the probes using the generator and then passes generated outputs to detectors.
   - Evaluators take the results from detectors as well as log data to produce a final aggregated report.
   - Finally, each part logs its activity for offline debugging and detailed audit (using log files and structured JSONL reports).

6. Important Architectural Patterns and Design Principles:
   - Modular, Plugin-Based Design: Each plugin category (probes, detectors, generators, etc.) has a clearly defined base class; new functionality is added by creating new plugins.
   - Separation of Concerns: The tool separates testing logic (probes and harnesses) from evaluation (detectors and evaluators), and from external model interfacing (generators).
   - Extensibility: The file and module structure makes it straightforward to add new attack vectors or support for additional LLM interfaces.
   - Testability: Extensive testing directories suggest that each component can be individually tested, supporting unit and integration tests.

7. Guidelines for Tailoring the Diagram:
   - For this full-stack security tool, clearly separate components into:
     • Frontend (CLI & User Input Parsing)
     • Core Testing Modules (Probes, Harnesses, Generators, Detectors, Evaluators)
     • Data/Configuration Layer (configs, data, resources)
     • Reporting & Logging (analysis, log files, JSON reports)
   - Focus the diagram on the flow from user input to vulnerability report, highlighting:
     • How the CLI triggers the controller.
     • The selection and orchestration of plugins.
     • The interactions with external LLM APIs (showing external service icons for OpenAI, Hugging Face, etc.).
     • The vertical flow from probing, through generation, detection, and evaluation, ending in output/log generation.

8. Instructing the Principal Software Engineer on Diagram Elements:
   - Use clearly labeled boxes for each component, such as “CLI/Entry Point”, “Probe Manager”, “Generator (LLM Interface)”, “Harness/Orchestrator”, “Detector Suite”, “Evaluator & Report Generator”, and “Data & Config Management”.
   - Include directional arrows to illustrate data flow:
     • From CLI to Controller.
     • Controller to Probes (which specify tests).
     • From Probes to Generator (communicating with external LLM service).
     • From Generator to Detectors (analysis of responses).
     • From Detectors to Evaluators, and finally to Logging/Reporting.
   - Consider color coding or using different shapes:
     • One color for user-facing/CLI components.
     • A separate color for backend processing modules (probes, detectors, generators).
     • Another for ancillary services (configuration, logging, external endpoints).
   - Ensure labels include technical details where relevant (e.g., “Plugin Base – Probes inherit from garak/probes/base.py”, “Multiple LLM interfaces supported: OpenAI, huggingface, ggml, etc.”).

By following these instructions, your diagram will capture the essential architecture of garak: from its modular, plugin-based design that integrates various testing modules with external LLM interfaces, to its robust logging and reporting system. This detailed view will not only help understand the component relationships but also assist in future enhancements or troubleshooting in the complex ecosystem of LLM vulnerability scanning.
</explanation>
